summary:
Both male and female same-sex sexual acts are criminal under national law in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code punishes any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural with six months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, equivalent to US$240 to US$720. Other sources report different maxima for the same conduct. The Human Dignity Trust profile gives up to three years imprisonment. A December 2024 press report cites Article 318 as carrying up to five years. The prior 1982 Penal Code provided up to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.

Enforcement against same-sex intimacy is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted and imprisoned after a sexual video showing him with another man was leaked online, described as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 Code. In June 2024 two women were detained after asking an imam to marry them. The request was not proven in court. The women stated they had previously engaged in sexual activity together. On 12 December 2024 a court convicted both of homosexuality and sentenced them to five and six months respectively, releasing them because detention since June exceeded the sentences. Reuters reported their release following the verdict.

A United States government human-rights report for 2023 stated that authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct that year and did not actively enforce the law. Police were reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, with no such violence reported in that year. This account predates the June to December 2024 detention and conviction.

Transgender persons are not permitted to change gender markers. No law protects against discrimination based on gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code provides no protections for LGBTQ persons. No general non-discrimination law exists.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition. The Family Code defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman.
tangentialFactors:
Government representatives have repeatedly refused recommendations from United Nations bodies to decriminalize homosexuality.

Broader reporting lists widespread impunity among major human-rights problems in Comoros. That context limits reliance on formal protection where enforcement is inconsistent.

Social stigma is reported among the broader population. A 2023 Gallup survey found 26 percent of respondents said the area where they lived would be a good place for LGBTQ+ people, an increase of 10 percentage points over the prior year.
localsOnly:
No LGBTIQ organisations are known to operate in Comoros. Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF of 1986 prohibits organisations founded on an unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose contrary to law or public morals, which chills registration and exposes such groups to potential prosecution.

Most LGBTQ+ people did not disclose sexual orientation or gender identity as of 2023. Reporting describes cultural discrimination and discrimination in access to education and employment. Some persons have been ostracized from homes, neighbourhoods and villages.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources disagree on the applicable penalty provision for same-sex conduct, citing Article 300 with six months to two years plus a fine, a three-year maximum, and Article 318 with up to five years. The inventory does not resolve which provision a court would apply.

No sourced information was available on entry or visa rules affecting trans visitors, on screening procedures that risk outing, on law governing access to bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, on access to gender-affirming care, or on hate-crime protection and its enforcement beyond the 2023 account of police conduct.

No documented statement on societal tolerance of transgender persons specifically was sourced. Trans-specific violence with dates and outcomes was not sourced.
